title: Can Place Flowers
description:
# Can Place Flowers

You are given a flowerbed represented by an integer array `flowerbed`. A `0` means the plot is empty, and a `1` means the plot already has a flower. Flowers cannot be planted in adjacent plots.

Return `true` if it is possible to plant exactly `n` new flowers without breaking the no-adjacent-flowers rule. Otherwise, return `false`.

The input flowerbed is already valid: it never contains two adjacent existing flowers.

## Example 1:

**Input:** flowerbed = [1,0,0,0,1], n = 1
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** Plant one flower in the middle empty plot.

## Example 2:

**Input:** flowerbed = [1,0,0,0,1], n = 2
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The middle run has room for only one new flower.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= flowerbed.length <= 2 * 10^4`
* `flowerbed[i]` is `0` or `1`.
* There are no two adjacent flowers in `flowerbed`.
* `0 <= n <= flowerbed.length`

solutions.name: Mutating Earliest-Plot Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the flowerbed from left to right. When the current plot is empty and both neighboring plots are either empty or outside the array, plant there immediately, decrement `n`, and keep scanning.

## Key Insight

Planting at the earliest legal plot cannot reduce the number of flowers that can be planted later: it only blocks the next plot, which would also be blocked by any legal placement starting farther right in the same empty run.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Zero-Run Capacity with Virtual Boundaries
solutions.description:
## Approach

Count consecutive zero runs instead of choosing positions one by one. Pretend there is one extra empty plot before the array and one after it, then every block of `zeros` available slots contributes `(zeros - 1) / 2` plantable positions.

## Key Insight

A run bounded by flowers needs one separator on each flower side. Adding virtual empty boundaries lets the same formula handle leading runs, trailing runs, all-empty beds, and runs between existing flowers.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Non-Mutating Last-Planted Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan left to right without modifying `flowerbed`. Track the index of the latest existing or virtually planted flower. An empty plot is usable when it is at least two positions after that index and the original right neighbor is not a flower.

## Key Insight

The left neighbor can be represented by `lastPlanted`, while the right neighbor must be checked in the original array. This keeps the greedy proof but avoids side effects on the caller's input.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Jumping Greedy Skip Blocked Plots
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a while loop and move the index by more than one when the local situation proves nearby plots cannot help. If the current plot already has a flower, skip the next plot. If a new flower is planted, also skip the next plot.

## Key Insight

Both an existing flower and a newly planted flower make the next plot illegal, so the scan can jump over it. This makes the blocking rule explicit and reduces the number of repeated neighbor checks.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Dynamic Programming Capacity Check
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute the maximum number of flowers that can still be planted from each index. The memoized state records the current index and whether the previous final plot is occupied by an existing or newly planted flower.

## Key Insight

This turns the problem into a local decision process: skip the current plot, or plant here only when the previous final plot is empty and the original next plot is not already occupied. The DP is heavier than greedy, but it is a useful correctness cross-check.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
